lines: Asha workers visit homes where the signal is weak or gone.
When something is wrong, they decide fast, alone.
A bleeding mother cannot wait for one bar of network.
Today, visits live on paper and in memory.
Protocols are long documents.
Help depends on a signal.
Urgent families are easy to miss.
Asha puts a safety check, a visit planner and approved protocol answers on the worker's own phone.
In Telugu and English, and it works offline.
Here is the whole app, end to end.
Ranked visits: who to attend first, by due dates, referrals and missed visits.
Households, with search, filters and new families.
Each house has an offline map and phone numbers.
Visits are saved offline and synced later.
Referrals, reports and alerts.
Settings for language, supervisor and voice.
On phones and tablets.
On the Ask page she can type or speak, in Telugu or English.
Her words fill the box.
She checks them, fixes a mistake, then presses Check.
Voice never sends anything on its own.
Offline engines come first. Online speech, only if she allows it.
Answers show their source, and medicine doses are refused.
Danger signs are checked first, by fixed rules, on the phone.
She types: bleeding in third trimester.
The rules flag a danger sign before any AI is asked.
On our test sets, every escalation case was caught, with no false alarms.
A clinician must still review the rules.
Answers come from a local AI on the server.
Ollama runs Qwen three to write the explanation, and B G E M three to find the approved text.
Short approved passages come back word for word.
Danger signs never wait for it.
We tested four Telugu voice options.
The phone's online speech was the most accurate, but needs internet.
Indic Conformer was fast, at a hundred and thirty eight megabytes.
Vosk was rejected.
Whisper won on size, not accuracy, because it keeps the app near a hundred megabytes.
So the worker always checks the words first.
The app is about fifty six megabytes.
Offline Telugu voice is an optional forty four megabyte download.
Phone numbers never leave the phone.
We tested on two sixty four bit phones.
Thirty two bit builds exist, and one and two gigabyte phones are the next test.
We tested the app, the safety rules, the retrieval and every voice option, on real phones.
Four hundred twenty seven automated app tests pass.
What is not done yet: the data is synthetic, and the rules await clinical review.
Asha. Works with zero bars.
